notes:
I've put together notes on 1 Chronicles 17, verse by verse, but some parts of your brief came up empty. I ran out of searches before finding anything on this chapter from Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran or Orthodox teachers, from Pentecostal teachers other than David Guzik on enduringword.com, or from bibleodyssey.org. I also found nothing about prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The one real Protestant disagreement I found is between Reformed and dispensational teachers. The notes follow.

**Overview**
- Guzik quotes Selman: this chapter is at the centre of how Chronicles tells Israel's history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Constable says the Davidic Covenant is the main theme of 1 Chronicles and the most important event in David's life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Carson (TGC) notes that the chapter closely follows 2 Samuel 7. The word "house" can mean a building or a household, and the play on both meanings is deliberate. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-chronicles-17-james-4-jonah-1-luke-6/

**Traditional reading, verse by verse**

v. 1:
- Guzik: cedar was a prized wood, so David's house was expensive. He was troubled that he lived better than the ark did. In effect he was proposing a temple to replace the tabernacle, which God had never asked for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Matthew Henry: David could not rest easy in his palace while the ark was in a tent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm
- Pulpit: finishing his own house showed David that the ark shouldn't stay in a tent. Nathan appears here with no introduction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm
- Cambridge Bible: 2 Samuel adds that God had given David rest from his enemies. The Chronicler probably dropped this because chapters 18–20 are about wars. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-1.htm

v. 2:
- Guzik: Nathan's answer was presumptuous, based on common sense before God had spoken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Pulpit: this was an on-the-spot reply. It wasn't entirely wrong, since God later says David's desire pleased Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm
- Ellicott: in Hebrew thought the heart was the seat of mind and will, not only feelings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html

v. 3:
- Pulpit: God's direct word came that same night and overruled human reasoning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm
- Precept Austin: Nathan was right that God was with David, but this plan was not God's will for him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-17-commentary

v. 4:
- Ellicott: the sense is "it is not you who will build the house." Samuel puts it as a question. The Chronicler writes "the house" because he has Solomon's Temple in mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Pulpit: "you" is stressed in the Hebrew, meaning someone else will build it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm
- Precept Austin, citing a NET note: the title "My servant" is kept for great spiritual leaders such as Moses, David, Hezekiah and the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-17-commentary

vv. 4–6, why God said no:
- Constable: mainly because God, not David, is sovereign. A secondary reason is that David was a man of war (1 Chr 22:8; 28:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Guzik gives the same "man of war" reason. He cites Spurgeon: God declined graciously and honoured David even while saying no. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Pulpit notes that the full reasons are given only in chapters 22 and 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm

vv. 5–6:
- Pulpit: God never asked any tribe or judge to build Him a house. He shared His people's wandering life without complaint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: God cares little for outward show in worship. He told the judges to feed His people, never to build Him a house. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm

vv. 7–8:
- Guzik: before making a promise that would be hard to believe, God reminds David of what He has already done for him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Keil & Delitzsch: "cut off all your enemies" means the enemies who had attacked him up to that time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-11.htm
- Ligonier sees grace in David being chosen while still a plain shepherd. https://ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/kingly-covenant

vv. 9–10:
- Guzik: God promised a secure Israel first, because David as a godly shepherd cared most about his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Ellicott: the opening of v. 10 really ends v. 9. It refers to oppression in the time of the judges and under Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Pulpit: "build you a house" means God guarantees an unbroken line of descendants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm

v. 11:
- Guzik: this promises a hereditary monarchy. No king of Israel had yet been followed by his son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Pulpit: Peter's words in Acts 2:29–30 come from this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-11.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch argue the Hebrew means one who comes *from David's sons*. That can't simply be Solomon, so it points to the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-13.htm

v. 12:
- Guzik: Solomon partly fulfilled this. David's line ruled for over 400 years, then a new Branch grew from Jesse's stump (Isa 11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Pulpit: these promises were kept for Solomon and were soon understood as prophecy (Ps 89, Isa 9, Heb 1:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm

v. 13:
- Ellicott: Chronicles leaves out Samuel's warning about punishing the son for sin. The prophecy looks past Solomon to the true Anointed One, to whom the warning couldn't apply. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Barnes gives a simpler reason: the writer isn't going to record Solomon's sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-13.htm
- Constable quotes a writer who calls this verse one of the Old Testament's main revelations of the Messiah's deity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Carson: when David's line sins, God's judgments will be temporary and the line will not be destroyed. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-chronicles-17-james-4-jonah-1-luke-6/

v. 14:
- TGC: Samuel says "your house and your kingdom." Chronicles says "My house and My kingdom," so the kingdom belongs to God. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/messianic-momentum-davidic-king/
- Precept Austin: God was Israel's true king, and David and Solomon ruled on His behalf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64071/
- Keil & Delitzsch: such words can only be said of the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-16.htm

v. 15:
- Ellicott: the substance comes from reliable tradition, but neither writer claims a word-for-word record. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html

v. 16:
- Guzik: David's attitude was that God is so great He gives gifts even to him, not that he was great. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Pulpit: "before the LORD" means before the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/17.htm

v. 17:
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is obscure, and Samuel has "this is the law of man." He suggests reading it as "a lesson for mankind." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html
- Pulpit: God treated David as if he were of very high rank. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-17.htm
- Henry mentions another reading that points to the Messiah "in the form of a man." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm

v. 18:
- Henry: the honour of being in covenant with God is so great that believers could wish for nothing more. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm
- Keil & Delitzsch argue the harder Chronicles wording is original. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-17.htm

v. 19:
- Henry: Samuel says "for Your word's sake," Chronicles "for Your servant's sake." Christ is both the Word and the Servant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-13.htm

vv. 20–21:
- Ellicott: Samuel adds "and their gods." The Chronicler may have dropped it because he saw pagan gods as nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html
- BibleHub's study notes: Israel was chosen out of God's love, not its greatness. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/17-21.htm

v. 22:
- NET note: literally, "you made your people Israel your own for a people permanently." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1Ch&chapter=17&verse=22

vv. 23–24:
- Guzik: David boldly asks God to do what He promised. It isn't passive prayer and it isn't arrogant prayer; it lays hold of the promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-17/
- Henry: God is the "God of Israel" in name and also "a God to Israel," living up to that name. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm
- Ligonier: David saw that keeping the promise would make God's own name great. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-thanks-the-lord

vv. 25–26:
- Precept Austin: David calls himself "servant" 10 times in 8 verses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64071/
- Ellicott: Chronicles leaves out Samuel's "and Your words are true." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html

v. 27:
- Henry: Samuel ends with a holy wish ("let it be blessed"). Chronicles ends with holy faith ("it will be blessed"). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_017.cfm
- Carson: for Jews living after the exile, this verse steadied them when their experience seemed to say the opposite. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-chronicles-17-james-4-jonah-1-luke-6/
- NET note: literally, "You… have blessed and [it is] blessed permanently." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1Ch&chapter=17&verse=27

**Where Protestant teachers differ (vv. 9–14)**
This split is between Reformed and dispensational teachers, not between denominations as such.
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Christ is already reigning on David's throne. Ligonier quotes Cyprian: the church is the temple David wanted to build. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-davidic and https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/eternal-covenant-david/
- **Reformed (Ligonier), on conditions:** the covenant has no conditions in that David will always have a son on the throne. It has conditions in that only an obedient son reigns forever, which Christ fulfils. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/throne-and-temple-zion/
- **Dispensational (John Walvoord, on bible.org):** the throne and kingdom are a literal, political rule over Israel. Christ now sits on the Father's throne, not David's, and the promise will be fulfilled in a future millennial reign. https://bible.org/seriespage/eschatological-problems-vii-fulfillment-davidic-covenant
- **Pulpit Homiletics** treats v. 9 as a promise to Israel still to be fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/17.htm
- **Constable** (also dispensational) says the covenant itself is unconditional, but its benefits depended on obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-17.html

**Catholic reading**
- Catholic Encyclopedia: the promise was a reward for David's piety. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/king-david
- Jimmy Akin: Judah had 20 kings over 450 years, all sons of David. After the exile, hope moved to a coming son of David. https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/for-450-years-every-king-came-from-one-family-heres-why
- Joe Heschmeyer: the promise isn't fulfilled in a worldly sense but in Christ. He also links it to the queen mother and Mary. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/what-the-davidic-kings-reveal-about-mary
- Haydock's Catholic commentary (on the page; no quotable excerpt available):
  - "Seed" runs down to Christ, born of the Virgin.
  - "Forever" can mean a long time, but Christ's rule has no end, and the Church inherits these promises.
  - On v. 13: Solomon may have repented, though this is uncertain.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/1_chronicles/17.htm

**Modern scholarship**
- On my sources, this comes only through Ellicott's comments on how Chronicles reworks Samuel (vv. 11, 15), and through Keil & Delitzsch, who argue against Bertheau and Thenius on 17:11–14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-17.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/17-13.htm
